This report synthesizes guidance from formal standards (ISO 17100:2015, ISO 18587:2017), industry bodies (GALA, TAUS, CSA Research), the MQM error taxonomy, Unicode infrastructure (CLDR, ICU MessageFormat), interoperability formats (XLIFF, W3C ITS), academic NMT research, and production QA tooling. The consistent finding across all of these sources is that preservation must be engineered at **four layers**: (1) declarative markup of what must be protected, (2) pipeline mechanisms that make protected content un-editable, (3) MT architecture that does not corrupt it, and (4) automated and human QA that catches residual violations before release. --- ## 1. The Three Preservation Classes and Why They Break ### 1.1 Named entities Brand names, product names, trademarks, person and place names, legal entity names, code identifiers, file paths, URLs, and API keys must typically survive translation untouched — or be rendered via a *documented, per-locale* transliteration decision. Unpreserved entities surface in quality evaluation as the MQM **Naming** error type ("incorrect name for a person, place, or organization") or as **Mistranslation** under Accuracy [1][2]. CSA Research positions protected naming as a brand-integrity issue: enterprises should define which names are never translated, test names per market for negative connotations and trademark conflicts, and centralize naming decisions so all vendors apply identical treatment [3]. ### 1.2 Numbers The cardinal rule, repeated across every source examined, is: **values are immutable; only formatting adapts.** A changed value (7% → 70%, 1,500 → 15,000, 1945 → 1995, 3.14 → 314) is a critical Mistranslation/Number error [1][2]; an adapted format (1,234.56 → 1.234,56) is correct locale handling. ISO 18587:2017 explicitly treats numbers, dates, and named entities as classic MT failure points that post-editors must verify even under light post-editing [4]. ### 1.3 Markup Inline tags, placeholders, and variables (`…`, `{0}`, `%s`, `%1$s`, `%@`, `{{name}}`, `${var}`, ``, ``) map to formatting, variables, and runtime behavior. MQM's **Design → Markup** category defines the failure: "target contains markup that is missing, incorrect, or does not correspond to the source markup" — e.g., unbalanced/dropped tags, a link tag around the wrong words, or "Clickhere" (missing space) [1][2]. Industry QA documentation identifies tag errors as among the most common causes of broken localized UIs and runtime crashes [5][6][7]. --- ## 2. The Governing Principle: Preserve the Value, Adapt the Format A crucial distinction runs through all authoritative sources — **preservation and localization are not opposites**: | Content | What may change | What must never change | |---|---|---| | Numbers | Separators, digit grouping, currency symbol/position, decimal digits, date order, calendar system | The numeric value itself | | Named entities | Script (per documented transliteration policy), name order conventions | The identity the name refers to | | Markup | Tag **position** (as target word order requires) | Tag **count, pairing, nesting order, and content** | Locale adaptation itself is governed by **Unicode CLDR**, the canonical locale-data repository covering **1,100+ locales**, used by ICU, Chrome, Android, Windows, macOS/iOS, Java, and .NET [8][9]. Key variation points include: - **Separators:** `1,234.56` (en) vs. `1.234,56` (de) vs. `1 234,56` (fr, narrow no-break space U+202F) vs. Arabic-Indic `١٬٢٣٤٫٥٦`; Indian 2-2-3 grouping (`1,23,45,678`); `minimumGroupingDigits=2` in es/it/pt [9][10]. - **~80 numbering systems** in CLDR (Latin, Arabic-Indic, Devanagari, Thai, Roman, Hebrew) [9][10]. - **Percent placement:** `50%` (en) vs. `50 %` (fr) vs. `%50` (tr) [10]. - **Currency:** JPY = 0 minor-unit digits, BHD/KWD = 3, most = 2; ambiguous symbols (`$`, `£`, `kr`) render as `US$` in en-CA but `$` in en-US; cash-rounding increments (e.g., CHF 0.05) [9][10]. - **Dates/calendars:** Gregorian plus Buddhist (th), Islamic, Persian (fa), Hebrew, Japanese imperial eras, Chinese lunar, Minguo; field order varies (`MMMM d, y` en-US; `d. MMMM y` de; `y年M月d日` ja) — never hardcode order or slice formatted strings [9][11]. - **Hour cycles** h11/h12 vs. h23/h24; first day of week; week-numbering rules [9][11]. ### 2.1 Plural rules: the hidden numeric trap CLDR defines up to **six plural categories** — `zero, one, two, few, many, other` — selected by rules over operands `n, i, v, w, f, t, e` [9][10]. Japanese/Chinese/Korean/Thai/Vietnamese use only `other`; English uses `one/other`; **Russian** uses `one/few/many/other` (1, 21… vs. 2–4, 22–24… vs. 0, 5–20…); **Arabic and Welsh use all six**; Irish uses five; **French has a `many`** category for large round numbers ("un million **d'**habitants") [10]. The engineering implication is absolute: code must use ICU `PluralRules`/MessageFormat — never `n == 1 ? "item" : "items"` — and translators must supply *every* category variant. GNU gettext encodes the same logic as per-language `Plural-Forms` expressions (`nplurals=3` for Russian) [12]. --- ## 3. Declarative Protection: Marking What Must Not Be Translated ### 3.1 W3C Internationalization Tag Set (ITS) **ITS 1.0** (W3C Recommendation, April 2007) defines six data categories — Translate, Localization Note, Terminology, Directionality, Language Information, Elements Within Text — via global rules (`its:rules` with XPath selectors) or local attributes [13]. **ITS 2.0** (W3C Recommendation, October 2013) adds ten more (16 total), including Domain, Text Analysis, Locale Filter, Preserve Space, Localization Quality Issue, and Provenance, with native HTML5 support (`translate`/`dir` attributes, `its-*` local attributes) [14]. Its practical effect: tools can **declaratively identify translatable vs. protected content** (e.g., `translate="no"`, script blocks, terminology) upstream of translation. ### 3.2 DNT lists and termbases (GALA / ISO 17100) GALA's guidance centers on **linguistic asset management**: build termbases with approved, banned, and conditional terms validated with client SMEs before kickoff; maintain **"Do Not Translate" (DNT) lists** for brand names, product names, trademarks, UI strings, and code identifiers; decide per locale whether proper nouns stay in source script or are transliterated — and record the decision [15]. ISO 17100:2015 mandates that terminology/glossaries, style guides, and reference materials be agreed **before production begins**, that client-supplied termbases be used with gaps flagged, and that source ambiguities (inconsistent names, unclear numbers) be **queried to the client rather than silently "corrected"** [16]. --- ## 4. Structural Carriers: XLIFF Inline Tags and ICU MessageFormat ### 4.1 XLIFF **XLIFF 1.2** (OASIS, February 2008) embeds five inline elements in ``/``: ``/`` (paired native codes, matched via `rid`/`id`), `` (standalone placeholder), `` (isolated begin/end), and `` (translatable content inside a code), with `ctype` and `equiv-text` attributes [17]. **XLIFF 2.x** (2.0 in 2014; 2.1 in 2019; 2.2 in 2020) redesigns the model: ``, `` (paired code containing content), ``/``, ``/``; native codes stored out-of-line in `` referenced by `dataRef`; and behavior controls — **`canCopy`, `canDelete`, `canReorder`** — that machine-enforce what a translator may do with a tag [18][19][20]. Android `strings.xml` embeds `` tags to mark non-translatable string parts [18]. ### 4.2 CAT-tool placeholder protection Format filters convert native markup — HTML/XML tags, printf (`%s`, `%1$s`), .NET (`{0}`), Java/ICU (`{name}`), Apple (`%@`), `${var}` — into **atomic inline tokens before segmentation**, so tokens are never split and translators cannot edit inside them. Typical protections: locked tags, insertion via shortcut, open/close pairing enforcement, auto-propagation, and QA verification for missing, extra, reordered, or empty tags (Trados Studio tag verification, memoQ QA, OmegaT validation, Phrase tag QA, Crowdin/Lokalise variable highlighting) [5][6][7]. ### 4.3 ICU MessageFormat **MessageFormat 1** syntax `{arg, type, style}` supports `number`, `date`, `time`, `spellout`, `ordinal`, `duration`, plus plural/select with CLDR categories and `#` for the formatted number [21]. **MessageFormat 2** — tech preview in ICU 75 (2024), **stable in ICU 76 (October 2024)** — adds declarations (`.input`, `.local`), `.match` selection, function placeholders (`{$count :number style=integer}`), defined error/fallback behavior, and **first-class markup parts** (open/close placeholders) so inline tags can be represented without breaking message syntax [22][23]. --- ## 5. MT Pipelines: Why Models Corrupt Preserved Content and How They Are Fixed ### 5.1 Documented failure modes - **Numbers:** Early NMT mapped rare tokens to ``; Luong et al. (2015) categorized rare-word errors (names, numbers) and showed post-hoc fixes recovering up to **≈ +2.8 BLEU** on WMT'14 [24]. BPE subword models (Sennrich et al., 2016) solved open vocabulary but split digit strings into **arbitrary fragments → dropped, duplicated, or mistranslated digits**, with verbatim copying even where locale conventions differ [25][26]. Koehn & Knowles (2017) listed rare words among six persistent NMT challenges [26]; Spithourakis & Riedel (2018) confirmed digit sequences are poorly modeled without format-aware treatment [27]. - **Names:** UNK omission, hallucination, inconsistent transliteration, or copying when an established target-language exonym exists; strong sensitivity to character-level noise (Belinkov & Bisk, 2018) [26][28]. - **Markup:** Models trained on plain text **delete, duplicate, misorder, or misnest tags** and corrupt placeholders; long-range reordering makes positional preservation hard [2][29]. ### 5.2 Architectural mitigations The literature converges on a layered recipe [24][25][29][30]: 1. **Copy/pointer mechanisms** — CopyNet (Gu et al., 2016), pointer-softmax (Gulcehre et al., 2016), pointer-generator (See et al., 2017); Umugwaneza et al. (AFRICON 2023) showed copy-augmented models improve retention of named entities, numbers, and OOV words for Kinyarwanda→English [31][32][33][34]. 2. **NER-driven placeholder masking** — detect entities, replace with type-tagged unique placeholders, re-insert after translation; Bunk et al. (2019) reported BLEU gains and fewer entity errors for English→German; Hoang et al. (2018) used entity masking during back-translation to force copying [35][36]. 3. **Hard terminology constraints** — lexically constrained decoding (Hokamp & Liu 2017; Post & Vilar 2018) and training models to apply glossaries via placeholder-style tokens (Dinu et al., 2019) [37][38][39]. 4. **Retrieval** — kNN-MT (Khandelwal et al., 2021) improves rare-token and entity consistency from translation memories [40]. 5. **Numeric post-validation** — no architectural fix fully eliminates digit and markup errors [27][2]. ### 5.3 Commercial-engine features Production engines operationalize these ideas as **glossaries/DNT enforcement** (Google Cloud Translation, Microsoft Translator, DeepL, ModernMT) — the pipeline-level equivalent of the DNT lists and constrained decoding described above [15][37][39]. --- ## 6. Enforcement: QA Workflows That Catch Violations ### 6.1 Automated QA checks Automated QA runs on bilingual files or TMS segments, flagging mechanical errors [5][6][7]: - **Tag/formatting mismatch** — missing, extra, duplicated, or reordered inline tags between source and target. - **Number mismatch** — compares numeric values source vs. target to catch dropped, altered, or mistranslated figures; advanced checkers **normalize for locale conventions** (decimal comma vs. point, digit grouping) to reduce false positives. - **Additional checks** — untranslated segments, source=target, terminology violations, forbidden characters, whitespace, capitalization, punctuation, URL/email integrity, length limits. Standard tools: **XBench** (de-facto industry standard, free), Trados Studio QA Checker, memoQ QA, Verifika, QA Distiller, and built-in QA in cloud TMS platforms (Phrase, Smartling, Crowdin, Lokalise, Transifex). Checks run (a) continuously as translators type, (b) as a gate before delivery to reviewers, and (c) as a final pre-release batch check, with errors triaged as real vs. false positive and re-run until zero critical errors remain [5][6][7]. ### 6.2 MQM: making preservation auditable The **Multidimensional Quality Metrics** framework makes preservation failures countable via explicit issue types [1][2][41]: | Failure | Full MQM tree | MQM 2021 revision | |---|---|---| | Wrong entity | Accuracy → Mistranslation; Locale convention → Person names | **Naming**: "incorrect name for a person, place, or organization" | | Wrong value | Accuracy → Mistranslation | **Number**: "numbers that do not match the source" | | Wrong format only | Locale convention → Number format | Locale convention | | Broken tags | Design → **Markup** | Design | **Severity is orthogonal to category**: Critical (renders text unusable; risk of physical, financial, legal, or reputational harm), Major (significantly disrupts comprehension/usability), Minor (detracts but does not impede), Neutral (zero penalty). Widely used default penalty weights are **Minor = 1, Major = 5, Critical = 25**; the WMT MQM protocol scores Minor = 1, Major = 5, treating Critical errors as extremely rare [41][42][43]. TAUS's Dynamic Quality Framework contributes a harmonized typology with matching categories (terminology, accuracy, locale convention) [44]. ### 6.3 Human LQA and sampling LQA is performed by a second linguist — the ISO 17100:2015 **two-person workflow** requires every translation to be checked by a second qualified linguist, explicitly covering accuracy, completeness, and terminology consistency [16]. Reviewers annotate errors with type and severity, apply weighted deductions, and compute a score (pass thresholds commonly around **95–99 points out of 100**); critical errors may trigger automatic failure regardless of total score. Because full review is expensive, LQA often uses sampling, with 100% review reserved for high-risk content (legal, medical, UI strings shipped to millions of users). Results feed back into training, glossary/style-guide updates, and MT post-editing rules [41][43][44]. ### 6.4 Pseudo-localization and regression testing Pseudo-locales machine-transform source strings **before real translations exist** [45][46][47]: - **Accented pseudo** (`en-XA`): maps ASCII to accented/exotic characters — reveals encoding bugs, missing glyphs, hardcoded strings. - **Expansion pseudo:** pads strings **~30–40% longer** (matching German/French growth), wrapped in delimiters (`[!!! Hëllô !!!]`) — reveals truncation, overflow, and **concatenation bugs** (brackets appearing mid-sentence). - **Pseudo-bidi** (`ar-XB`): substitutes RTL-looking characters and inserts directional marks — surfaces bidi/layout/mirroring bugs. Pseudo runs verify that placeholders (`{0}`, `%s`, `{{name}}`) and ICU patterns survive intact. Xcode ships Double-Length, Accented, and Right-to-Left pseudolanguages; Android exposes en-XA/ar-XB in developer options [45][47]. **Limits:** pseudo-locales still use English plural rules and don't test real Arabic shaping or Russian plural categories — complement with snapshot tests against real locales (de-DE, ar-EG, ru-RU, ja-JP, hi-IN) [45]. Post-integration regression testing verifies per-language builds: UI strings fit containers, variables render at runtime, hotkeys don't collide in translated labels, and localized resources load without missing-key errors — automated via screenshot comparison per locale, locale-parameterized UI frameworks (Selenium, Appium, Playwright), string-length assertions, and untranslated-English "leak" detection, gated in CI/CD [48][49]. --- ## 7. Consolidated Best-Practice Checklist **Named entities** - Inventory entity classes; decide keep/transliterate/translate **per locale** and record the decision [15][3]. - Store as DNT or termbase entries; load glossary with DNT flags in the CAT tool; copy strings exactly (casing, spacing, hyphenation) [15][50]. - Verify against authoritative sources; auto-check DNT strings; watch for false look-alikes ("Finder," "Edge," "Swift") [50]. **Numbers** - Adapt *format* to locale (per CLDR) but never alter *values*; diff source vs. target digit-by-digit [9][50]. - Apply correct separators, currency symbol/position/decimal digits (JPY = 0, KWD = 3); disambiguate `$` with ISO code where specified [10][50]. - Protect numbers that must not be reformatted (version numbers, serials, phone numbers, postal codes, legal references); disable autoformat interference [50]. - Use full CLDR plural categories — never concatenate number + fixed noun [10][12]. **Markup** - Preserve all inline tags; tag count and pairing must match source even when position shifts; never break nesting order — orphan tags are the #1 cause of build failures [5][50]. - Translate only translatable attribute values (`alt`, `title`, `aria-label`); never touch element/attribute names, `id`/`class`, or `

Checks run (a) continuously as translators type, (b) as a gate before delivery to reviewers, and (c) as a final pre-release batch check, with errors triaged as real vs. false positive and re-run until zero critical errors remain [5][6][7]. ### 6.2 MQM: making preservation auditable The **Multidimensional Quality Metrics** framework makes preservation failures countable via explicit issue types [1][2][41]: | Failure | Full MQM tree | MQM 2021 revision | |---|---|---| | Wrong entity | Accuracy → Mistranslation; Locale convention → Person names | **Naming**: "incorrect name for a person, place, or organization" | | Wrong value | Accuracy → Mistranslation | **Number**: "numbers that do not match the source" | | Wrong format only | Locale convention → Number format | Locale convention | | Broken tags | Design → **Markup** | Design | **Severity is orthogonal to category**: Critical (renders text unusable; risk of physical, financial, legal, or reputational harm), Major (significantly disrupts comprehension/usability), Minor (detracts but does not impede), Neutral (zero penalty). Widely used default penalty weights are **Minor = 1, Major = 5, Critical = 25**; the WMT MQM protocol scores Minor = 1, Major = 5, treating Critical errors as extremely rare [41][42][43]. TAUS's Dynamic Quality Framework contributes a harmonized typology with matching categories (terminology, accuracy, locale convention) [44]. ### 6.3 Human LQA and sampling LQA is performed by a second linguist — the ISO 17100:2015 **two-person workflow** requires every translation to be checked by a second qualified linguist, explicitly covering accuracy, completeness, and terminology consistency [16]. Reviewers annotate errors with type and severity, apply weighted deductions, and compute a score (pass thresholds commonly around **95–99 points out of 100**); critical errors may trigger automatic failure regardless of total score. Because full review is expensive, LQA often uses sampling, with 100% review reserved for high-risk content (legal, medical, UI strings shipped to millions of users). Results feed back into training, glossary/style-guide updates, and MT post-editing rules [41][43][44]. ### 6.4 Pseudo-localization and regression testing Pseudo-locales machine-transform source strings **before real translations exist** [45][46][47]: - **Accented pseudo** (`en-XA`): maps ASCII to accented/exotic characters — reveals encoding bugs, missing glyphs, hardcoded strings. - **Expansion pseudo:** pads strings **~30–40% longer** (matching German/French growth), wrapped in delimiters (`[!!! Hëllô !!!]`) — reveals truncation, overflow, and **concatenation bugs** (brackets appearing mid-sentence). - **Pseudo-bidi** (`ar-XB`): substitutes RTL-looking characters and inserts directional marks — surfaces bidi/layout/mirroring bugs. Pseudo runs verify that placeholders (`{0}`, `%s`, `{{name}}`) and ICU patterns survive intact. Xcode ships Double-Length, Accented, and Right-to-Left pseudolanguages; Android exposes en-XA/ar-XB in developer options [45][47]. **Limits:** pseudo-locales still use English plural rules and don't test real Arabic shaping or Russian plural categories — complement with snapshot tests against real locales (de-DE, ar-EG, ru-RU, ja-JP, hi-IN) [45]. Post-integration regression testing verifies per-language builds: UI strings fit containers, variables render at runtime, hotkeys don't collide in translated labels, and localized resources load without missing-key errors — automated via screenshot comparison per locale, locale-parameterized UI frameworks (Selenium, Appium, Playwright), string-length assertions, and untranslated-English "leak" detection, gated in CI/CD [48][49]. --- ## 7.
